subject: iron lung
title: What If a Machine Had to Breathe for You for 70 Years? One Man's Did

scenes.text: What if a machine had to breathe for you, for seventy years? For one man it did.
Texas, 1952. Polio leaves six-year-old Paul Alexander paralysed from the neck down, unable to breathe on his own.
He's put in an iron lung: a seven-foot metal cylinder that uses air pressure to draw air into his lungs.
He teaches himself to breathe by gulping air down. Three minutes on his own would earn him a dog. It took a year.
Those gulps buy him hours outside the machine. Enough for college, law school, and thirty years as a courtroom lawyer.
He typed a memoir with a stick held in his mouth. Guinness named him the longest-surviving iron lung patient. He died in 2024, aged 78.

description:
What if a machine had to breathe for you for seventy years? For Paul Alexander of Texas, it did.
Polio paralysed him from the neck down in 1952, at the age of six, and he relied on an iron lung, a metal cylinder that uses changes in air pressure to move air in and out of the lungs, for more than 70 years. He learned to breathe on his own for hours at a time by swallowing air, earned a law degree and practised as an attorney for 30 years. Guinness World Records recognised him in 2023 as the longest-surviving iron lung patient. He died in March 2024, aged 78.
